item.mechanism: Mechanical alloying induces lattice strain and crystal size refinement through severe cold working and work hardening, leading to the formation of a supersaturated solid solution with nanocrystalline grains.
item.system: CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy powders milled for 1 to 6 hours
item.operating_conditions: High–energy ball milling (QM–1SP4), 400 rpm, argon atmosphere, milling durations 1 h to 6 h
item.supporting_observation: XRD peak broadening and intensity reduction, SEM showing particle size decrease from 100 µm to 30 µm, and hardness increase from 525 HV to 675 HV.
item.scope_limits: The text notes that HCP phase formation was observed at 3 h but disappeared by 4 h; the mechanism of grain refinement is specific to the milling duration and intensity described.
item.alternatives_considered: Casting method which leads to porosity and non-homogeneous microstructure; conventional sintering methods which are time-consuming.
quotes: The intense collisions during the process induced significant cold working and work hardening effects in the particles
The diminishing average particle size over prolonged milling periods underscores the dominance of the fracture process over cold welding
This increasing in hardness resulted from grain refinement and enhanced dislocation density due to prolonged milling

item.mechanism: Phase stability and the formation of dual FCC/BCC structures are governed by thermodynamic parameters including mixing enthalpy, mixing entropy, atomic size difference, and valence electron concentration (VEC).
item.operating_conditions: Predicted via Hume–Rothery rules and thermodynamic calculations prior to synthesis; VEC = 7.2, δ = 6.15
item.supporting_observation: Thermodynamic parameters predicted the emergence of solid solution structures encompassing both FCC and BCC; VEC of 7.2 falls within the range 6.87 ≤ VEC ≤ 8.
item.scope_limits: The text states that the influence of VEC on phase stability between amorphous and solid solution phases can be ignored in this specific context, though it is crucial for FCC vs BCC selection.
item.alternatives_considered: Single-phase FCC or BCC structures; amorphous phase formation.
quotes: VEC is crucial in dictating the formation of solid solutions in high–entropy alloys (HEAs), with the FCC structure forming when the VEC was 8 or higher, and the BCC structure emerging when the VEC was below 6.87
The valence electron concentration (VEC) was 7.2, falling within the range of 6.87 ≤ VEC ≤ 8, suggesting the phase forming of both face–centered cubic (FCC) and body–centered cubic (BCC) structures
Collectively, these thermodynamic parameters predicted the emergence of solid solution structures encompassing both FCC and BCC

item.mechanism: The formation kinetics of FCC and BCC phases follow a nucleation and growth mechanism, where FCC nucleation is delayed (approx. 5 h) while BCC nucleation and growth occur simultaneously from the start.
item.system: CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy during mechanical alloying
item.operating_conditions: Ball milling times from 0 h to 6 h; analyzed using Johnson–Mehl–Avrami (JMA) model
item.supporting_observation: Avrami exponent analysis showed interface-controlled growth; FCC nucleation time approx 5 h, BCC had no obvious nucleation time.
item.scope_limits: The kinetic model assumes time-independent Avrami exponent and rate constant; specific to the milling process described.
item.alternatives_considered: Diffusion-controlled mechanism; reaction-controlled mechanism; homogeneous vs heterogeneous nucleation.
quotes: The α(t) plot indicates an approximate nucleation time of about 5 h for the FCC solid solution
Conversely, for the BCC phase, there was no obvious nucleation time, suggesting that the nucleation and growth happened simultaneously with the milling process
The Avrami exponent (n) indicates that the formation kinetics of the CuCrFeTiNi high–entropy alloy (HEA) are primarily governed by interface–controlled growth mechanisms

item.mechanism: High hardness and strength are achieved through the synergistic effect of refined microstructure, solid solution strengthening, and the significant proportion of the BCC phase.
item.system: Bulk CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy sintered via SPS
item.operating_conditions: Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 900 °C to 1000 °C for 10 min; compressive testing at room temperature
item.supporting_observation: Vickers hardness reached 675 Hv; compressive strength 1894 MPa; yield stress 1238 MPa.
item.scope_limits: The text notes that the alloy exhibited brittle behavior in some contexts and that high strength correlates with low ductility due to nanoprecipitates.
item.alternatives_considered: Commercial alloys like Stellite (500 Hv) and nickel/cobalt–based superalloys which showed lower hardness.
quotes: This elevated hardness can be attributed to the refined microstructure, solid solution strengthening effects, and the significant proportion of the BCC phase within the alloy
The enhanced hardness can be attributed to the high titanium content, which induced lattice expansion
The bulk CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy exhibited a remarkable hardness value of 675 Hv, surpassing that of most commercial alloys

item.mechanism: Densification during sintering is driven by atomic diffusion and particle rearrangement, which are thermally activated processes dependent on sintering temperature.
item.operating_conditions: SPS sintering temperatures: 950 °C, 1000 °C, 1050 °C; heating rate 50 °C/min; hold time 10 min
item.supporting_observation: Density increased from 6.57 g/cm³ at 950 °C to 6.98 g/cm³ at 1050 °C; compaction rate increased with temperature.
item.scope_limits: At low temperatures (950 °C), atomic diffusion is suppressed leading to micropores; saturation effect may occur at very high temperatures.
item.alternatives_considered: Conventional sintering methods which are slower; hot pressing.
quotes: Due to the suppression of atomic diffusion at low temperatures, there is a decrease in the interaction between powder particles during the sintering process
A higher sintering temperature can enhance the compaction rate, but there may be a saturation effect at very high temperatures
This was consistent with the fundamental principles of sintering, where higher temperatures provide more energy for particle rearrangement, diffusion, and bonding

item.mechanism: Elemental segregation occurs during mechanical alloying where Fe, Cr, and Ti tend to form solid solutions within the BCC phase, while Co and Ni tend to form solid solutions within the FCC phase.
item.system: CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy powder after 6 h milling
item.operating_conditions: Mechanical alloying for 6 h; analyzed via EDS mapping and line scanning
item.supporting_observation: EDS MAP analysis showed uniform distribution of Fe, Ti, Cr but distinct distribution for Co and Ni; two distinct patterns correspond to FCC and BCC phases.
item.scope_limits: The text mentions a higher proportion of iron in the powder; the segregation pattern is specific to the final milled state.
item.alternatives_considered: Uniform distribution of all elements (which was achieved in terms of overall homogeneity but distinct at phase level).
quotes: According to this analysis, elements such as Fe, Ti, and Cr exhibited a uniform distribution, whereas Co and Ni displayed a distinct distribution pattern

Due to their intrinsic crystal structures, elements such as Fe, Cr, and Ti exhibited a tendency to form solid solutions within the BCC phase, whereas Co and Ni were more inclined to form solid solutions within the FCC phase
The two distinct distribution patterns observed in the final sample correspond to the FCC and BCC phases, respectively

item.mechanism: The dual-phase microstructure (FCC + BCC) provides a balanced combination of elevated strength (from BCC) and flexibility (from FCC), superior to single-phase alloys.
item.system: CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy with dual-phase structure
item.operating_conditions: Post-milling and sintering; room temperature mechanical testing
item.supporting_observation: The alloy exhibited exceptional strength (1894 MPa) while maintaining some plasticity; the text explicitly links dual-phase to balanced properties.
item.scope_limits: Single-phase BCC lacks flexibility; single-phase FCC is weaker; the balance is specific to the CoCrFeNiTi composition.
item.alternatives_considered: Single-phase FCC or BCC structures; amorphous structures.
quotes: High–entropy alloys (HEAs) with body–centered cubic (BCC) structures are renowned for their remarkable strength, yet they lack the flexibility inherent in other alloy types
In stark contrast, HEAs exhibiting face–centered cubic (FCC) structures, while weaker in terms of strength, offer superior flexibility

For achieving the balanced combination of elevated strength and flexibility, alloys often require a dual–phase microstructure integrating face–centered cubic (FCC) and body–centered cubic (BCC) phases

item.mechanism: Intergranular fracture and the presence of nanoprecipitates contribute to high strength but result in low ductility.
item.system: Bulk CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy sintered at 900–1000 °C
item.operating_conditions: Compressive testing; fracture morphology analysis via SEM
item.supporting_observation: Fracture morphologies showed intergranular fracture; regions of deformation marked by arrows confirmed nanoprecipitate role.
item.scope_limits: The text notes low ductility associated with this mechanism; specific to the sintered bulk material.
quotes: The SPS–processed CoCrFeNiTi HEA underwent intergranular fracture
Additionally, the regions of deformation are marked by arrows, which confirms that nanoprecipitates play an important role in high strength and low ductility
